sections.title: The five verb forms
sections.summary: Every English verb has up to five forms. All tenses are built from them.

tables.caption: The five forms of a regular verb and an irregular verb
head: Form
Work (regular)
Write (irregular)
Used for
rows: present simple (I, you, we, they), infinitive, after modals

uses: Regular verbs add -ed for the past simple and the past participle. The two forms are the same.
Irregular verbs have their own past simple and past participle. Learn them in the Irregular verbs glossary.
Add -es to the -s form when the verb ends in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o (watches, goes). A consonant plus -y becomes -ies (studies).
Before -ing, drop a silent -e (make, making). Double a final consonant after one short vowel (run, running).

examples.text: She works in a bank.
He wrote an email.
examples.note: past simple of an irregular verb

examples.text: I have written three emails today.
They are running in the park.

mistakes.wrong: She work in a bank.
mistakes.why: After he, she and it, the present simple needs the -s form.

mistakes.wrong: I have wrote the letter.
mistakes.why: After have, use the past participle (written), not the past simple (wrote).

checks.question: What is the -ing form of the verb run?
checks.explanation: Run ends in one short vowel and one consonant, so the consonant doubles.

checks.question: What is the -s form of the verb study?
checks.explanation: A consonant plus -y changes to -ies.

sections.title: Present simple
sections.summary: Use the present simple for habits, facts and timetables.

tables.caption: Present simple of the verb work
head: Affirmative
Negative
Question

uses: A habit or routine: I get up at seven every day.
A fact that is always true: Water boils at 100 degrees.
A timetable or schedule: The train leaves at 9.15.
A state: She likes tea. He knows the answer.

examples.text: My brother plays tennis on Saturdays.
Do you live near the school?
The shop doesn't open on Sundays.
examples.note: After doesn't, use the base form (open), without -s.

mistakes.wrong: Does she works here?
mistakes.why: Does already shows the -s. The main verb stays in the base form.

mistakes.wrong: I am go to school by bus.
mistakes.right: I go to school by bus.
mistakes.why: Do not use am, is or are with a base form for a habit.

checks.question: Complete: He ___ (not / like) coffee.
checks.explanation: Negative with he: doesn't plus the base form.

checks.question: Complete: ___ your sister play the piano?
checks.explanation: Questions with she use does plus the base form.

sections.title: Present continuous
sections.summary: Use the present continuous for actions that happen now or around now, and for fixed plans.

tables.caption: Present continuous of the verb work
head: Affirmative
Negative
Question

uses: An action that is happening now: Be quiet, the baby is sleeping.
A temporary situation: I am staying with my aunt this week.
A changing situation: The weather is getting colder.
A fixed plan in the near future: We are meeting Tom at six.

examples.text: She is talking to the teacher right now.
Are you using this chair?
I am flying to Dublin tomorrow.
examples.note: A plan with a fixed time.

mistakes.wrong: I am knowing the answer.
mistakes.why: Verbs of state (know, like, want, understand, believe) do not usually take the continuous.

mistakes.wrong: She is work at the moment.
mistakes.right: She is working at the moment.
mistakes.why: After am, is or are, use the -ing form.

checks.question: Complete: Look! It ___ (rain).
checks.explanation: Look! shows that the action is happening now.

checks.question: Choose the correct sentence: 'I am wanting a coffee.' or 'I want a coffee.'
checks.explanation: Want is a verb of state and does not usually take the continuous.

sections.title: Past simple
sections.summary: Use the past simple for finished actions at a known time in the past.

tables.caption: Past simple of the verbs work (regular) and go (irregular)
head: Affirmative
Negative
Question

uses: A finished action at a definite time: We visited Paris in 2022.
A series of actions in a story: He opened the door, looked inside and left.
A past habit or state that is finished: When I was a child, I lived in a village.

examples.text: I met my best friend at school.
Did you see the match last night?
They didn't arrive on time.
examples.note: After didn't, use the base form (arrive).

mistakes.wrong: Did you went to the party?
mistakes.right: Did you go to the party?
mistakes.why: Did already shows the past. The main verb stays in the base form.

mistakes.wrong: I have seen him yesterday.
mistakes.why: With a finished time word such as yesterday, use the past simple, not the present perfect.

checks.question: Complete: She ___ (not / call) me last night.
checks.explanation: Negative past simple: didn't plus the base form.

checks.question: What is the past simple of the verb buy?
checks.explanation: Buy is irregular: buy, bought, bought.

sections.title: Past continuous
sections.summary: Use the past continuous for an action that was in progress at a time in the past.

tables.caption: Past continuous of the verb work
head: Affirmative
Negative
Question

uses: An action in progress at a moment in the past: At eight o'clock I was having dinner.
A longer action that was interrupted by a shorter action (past simple): I was walking home when it started to rain.
Two actions in progress at the same time: She was cooking while he was reading.

examples.text: We were waiting for the bus when we saw an accident.
What were you doing at nine o'clock?
He wasn't listening to the teacher.
examples.note: The action was in progress, so we use the continuous.

mistakes.wrong: While I walked home, it started to rain.
mistakes.right: While I was walking home, it started to rain.
mistakes.why: The longer action in progress needs the past continuous.

mistakes.wrong: I was knowing his name.
mistakes.why: Verbs of state do not usually take the continuous.

checks.question: Complete: I ___ (sleep) when the phone rang.
checks.explanation: The sleeping was in progress when the phone rang.

checks.question: Complete: They ___ (play) football when it began to snow.
checks.explanation: Use were with they and the -ing form for the action in progress.

sections.title: Present perfect
sections.summary: Use the present perfect to link the past with now: experience, recent news and unfinished time.

tables.caption: Present perfect of the verb work
head: Affirmative
Negative
Question

uses: Life experience, with no time given: I have been to Italy twice.
A recent action with a result now: I have lost my keys (I can't get in).
An action that started in the past and continues now (with for and since): She has lived here for ten years.
Unfinished time periods: I have seen three films this week.

examples.text: Have you ever eaten sushi?
He has just left the office.
We have known each other since 2015.
examples.note: Since + a point in time. For + a length of time (for ten years).

mistakes.wrong: I have visited Rome last year.
mistakes.why: A finished time (last year) needs the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: She has went home.
mistakes.why: After have or has, use the past participle (gone), not the past simple (went).

checks.question: Complete: I ___ (live) here since 2018.
checks.explanation: The situation started in the past and continues now. Since 2018 gives the start point.

checks.question: What is the past participle of the verb take?
checks.explanation: Take is irregular: take, took, taken.

sections.title: Future: will and going to
sections.summary: Use will for decisions made now and predictions. Use going to for plans and for predictions with evidence.

tables.caption: Forms of will and going to
head: Affirmative
Negative
Question

uses: Will: a decision at the moment of speaking. The phone is ringing. I'll answer it.
Will: a prediction based on opinion. I think it will rain tomorrow.
Will: a promise or an offer. I'll carry your bag.
Going to: a plan or intention. We are going to buy a new car.
Going to: a prediction with evidence now. Look at the sky! It is going to rain.

examples.text: I'll have the soup, please.
She is going to study medicine.
Be careful! You are going to fall.
examples.note: The evidence is in front of you.

mistakes.wrong: She will to call you.
mistakes.why: After will, use the base form without to.

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay at home.
mistakes.right: If it rains, we will stay at home.
mistakes.why: After if, use the present simple, not will.

checks.question: Complete: 'I'm cold.' 'I ___ (close) the window.'
checks.explanation: A decision made at the moment of speaking uses will ('ll).

checks.question: Complete: We ___ (visit) my grandparents next month. We have bought the tickets.
checks.explanation: A plan that is already made uses going to.

sections.title: Passive voice
sections.summary: Use the passive when the action is more important than the person who does it, or when we do not know who did it.
uses: The person who does the action is not known or not important: The window was broken.
The result is more important than the person: The bridge was built in 1990.
Use by plus the person when it is useful: The book was written by a student.

examples.text: English is spoken in many countries.
The thief was caught by the police.
My phone has been repaired.

mistakes.wrong: The letter was wrote yesterday.
mistakes.why: The passive needs the past participle (written).

mistakes.wrong: The film was happened in Spain.
mistakes.right: The film was made in Spain. / The accident happened in Spain.
mistakes.why: Verbs without an object (happen, arrive, die) have no passive.

checks.question: Make it passive: They built this school in 1980.
checks.explanation: Past simple passive: was or were plus the past participle.

checks.question: Complete: The room ___ (clean) every day.
checks.explanation: Present simple passive: is or are plus the past participle.

sections.title: Modal verbs
sections.summary: Modal verbs show ability, permission, advice, obligation and possibility. They are followed by the base form.

tables.caption: Common modal verbs at B1
head: Modal
Meaning
Example
rows: I can swim. Could you help me?
You must stop. I have to work tomorrow.

uses: Modals have no -s in the third person: she can, he must.
Questions and negatives do not use do: Can you swim? I can't swim.
Use have to (not must) in the past: I had to leave early.
Might is less sure than may. Both are about possibility now or in the future.

examples.text: You should drink more water.
Students mustn't use phones in the exam.
You don't have to wear a suit.
examples.note: It is not necessary, but it is allowed.

mistakes.wrong: She cans swim very well.
mistakes.why: Modals never take -s.

mistakes.wrong: You should to go home.
mistakes.why: After a modal, use the base form without to.

checks.question: Complete: You ___ smoke in the hospital. It is forbidden.
checks.explanation: Mustn't means that something is forbidden.

checks.question: Complete: I ___ finish my report today. It is the deadline. (obligation)
checks.explanation: Must or have to show a strong obligation.

sections.title: First conditional
sections.summary: Use the first conditional for real or possible situations in the future and their results.
uses: A possible future situation and its likely result.
A warning, a promise or an offer: If you touch it, you will get hurt.
The if clause can come first or second. Use a comma only when the if clause comes first.
Unless means if not: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train.

examples.text: If I see Anna, I will tell her.
We won't go out if it snows.
What will you do if you don't get the job?

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, I will take an umbrella.
mistakes.right: If it rains, I will take an umbrella.
mistakes.why: Do not use will in the if clause.

mistakes.wrong: If I will see him, I tell him.
mistakes.right: If I see him, I will tell him.
mistakes.why: The if clause uses the present simple. The main clause uses will.

checks.question: Complete: If she ___ (come), we will start.
checks.explanation: The if clause uses the present simple.

checks.question: Complete: If you heat ice, it ___ (melt).
checks.explanation: For a general truth, both clauses use the present simple (zero conditional).

sections.title: Second conditional
sections.summary: Use the second conditional for unreal or unlikely situations in the present or future, and for advice.

tables.caption: Structure of the second conditional
head: if clause
main clause
rows: we would see her more often.

uses: An unreal or very unlikely situation: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
Advice, with if I were you: If I were you, I would take the job.
Use were for all persons in a formal style: If he were taller, he would play basketball.

examples.text: If I had a car, I would drive to work.
What would you do if you lost your passport?
If I were you, I would talk to the teacher.
examples.note: A common way to give advice.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have time, I would help you.
mistakes.right: If I had time, I would help you.
mistakes.why: Do not use would in the if clause. Use the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: If I was rich, I will buy a boat.
mistakes.right: If I were rich, I would buy a boat.
mistakes.why: The main clause needs would, not will, for an unreal situation.

checks.question: Complete: If I ___ (know) the answer, I would tell you.
checks.explanation: The if clause uses the past simple, but the meaning is present.

checks.question: Complete: She ___ (travel) more if she had more money.
checks.explanation: The main clause of the second conditional uses would plus the base form.
